newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan investor bids seen limited at U.S. refunding.
newsitem.headline: Japan investor bids seen limited at U.S. refunding.

text.p: Japanese institutional investors may not stand out at this week's U.S. quarterly refunding, but this should not be taken to mean they have lost their appetite for foreign bond assets, traders said on Monday.
"In general, Japanese investors' desire to bid actively at the refunding faded long ago," said Michihisa Tanimoto, foreign bond and forex section manager at Sumitomo Life Insurance Co.
"There is no definite need to stand out at the auction because the investors can always buy (in the secondary market)."
"We'll keep our stance by investing in Treasuries of maturities up to about five years," he said.
The Treasury Department announced a $39.75 billion quarterly refunding last Wednesday.
The auctions will consist of $17.75 billion of three-year notes on Tuesday, $12 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday.
"Considering (February 11) is a Japanese holiday, there is a possibility that they may refrain from taking part in the auction altogether," said a senior manager at a major Japanese brokerage.

But traders added that cash-rich Japanese investors are still poised to boost their foreign bond holdings, particularly U.S. Treasuries, as they see the dollar's bullish trend continuing despite the weekend Group of Seven (G7) meeting that called for stable exchange rates.
"If the Japanese are to participate, I think three-year notes would have some demand, but I have doubts about the longer term ones," the brokerage manager said.
In the 1980s, Japanese institutional investors were main buyers at the refundings, often seen buying about 30 to 40 percent at an auction, traders said.
In the early 1990s, investors reduced their foreign bond holdings as their profits were severely battered as a result of the yen's rise against the dollar at the time.
But in recent years, institutional investors have put their money in offshore bonds as they seek higher returns at a time of ultra-low domestic rates and a sagging yen, traders said.
"So far, the depreciating trend of the yen (against the dollar) has created favourable environment for investing into the Treasury market," one official at a public fund said.
But he declined to comment whether the public fund will bid at the quarterly refunding.
On Monday, the Ministry of Finance said that the net purchase of foreign bonds by Japanese investors rose to 8.40 trillion yen in 1996, the fifth highest amount ever.
Last week, Tokyo currency dealers said that a major Japanese public fund was spotted buying substantial amounts of U.S. government notes in the market.
